lines: My mother haggled the way other people pray: with total concentration and a faint look of disappointment in everyone present.
On Saturdays I trailed behind her through the vegetable market in Karachi, learning the grammar of a bargain.
First, the insult, delivered with love.
Then the vendor's cry, half pain, half applause.
I wanted to pay the price on the sign and go home, like the people in the television advertisements.
I asked once, in the rickshaw, tomatoes in my lap.
She looked at me for a long time.
"And because when I stop, he will think I have stopped seeing him."
It took me twenty years to understand that she was never bargaining for the tomatoes.
Last month I stood in a supermarket in Toronto, reading a price I could not argue with, and felt something close to grief.
I put the tomatoes in the basket.
I said a small rude word to them, tenderly, in my mother's voice.
